proof:
The continuous normals sum to zero. On the closed opposite polyhedron, summing the three inequalities of each row and of the cross-triple gives four nonnegative affine functions:
$$
-3+12z_1+12z_2,\quad 13-16z_1+10z_2,\quad
13+10z_1-16z_2,\quad 13-8z_1-8z_2.
$$
Writing $s=z_1+z_2$, these force $1/4\le s\le13/8$ and
$$
(16s-13)/26\le z_1\le(13+10s)/26.
$$
At an integer base $s=1$, but then $3/26\le z_1\le23/26$ is impossible. These intervals also bound the base; the three complementary inequalities of row 0 bound the continuous coordinates over this bounded set, because their normals positively span $\mathbb R^2$. At $z=(1/2,1/2)$ each threshold is at least one, so $x=0$ is strictly feasible. Each integer base violates one of the four summed complementary inequalities strictly, and the corresponding three open caps cover its entire plane.

At $A,B,C$ the thresholds in their own rows $0,1,2$ are all $-1$, and every other threshold there is at least three. The three vertices of $K$ in the stated order have normal values $5/2$ for their indexed normal and $-5/4$ for the other two. Thus at the own base of cap $(g,i)$ its indexed vertex lies strictly in that cap and strictly outside the other eight. The line segment from this witness to the strict feasible point meets the deleted inequality's boundary while all other inequalities remain strict. This proves each inequality is a facet and each cap is indispensable.

A minimal positive dependence must include one copy of each direction, with equal weights; all $3^3=27$ such choices work. At a fixed base such a triple covers the whole plane by its closed caps precisely when its threshold sum is nonpositive. To verify necessity, if the sum is positive take $x$ whose three normal values equal the three thresholds less their positive average. The values sum to zero, so they are realized by the map $x\mapsto(x_1,x_2,-x_1-x_2)$, and this point misses all three caps. Sufficiency follows by summing the margins. At $A,B,C$ the respective own rows have sum $-3$, whereas any replacement makes the sum at least $-1-1+3=1$. At $D$ the three threshold rows are $(7,7,7)$, $(13,-5,-1)$, $(13,-1,-5)$. In each direction the unique smallest entries give $(7,-5,-5)$ with sum $-3$; any replacement gives sum at least one. Thus all four named groups are forced, and the cross-triple has no private cap even if more groups are used.

The convex source projects to the binary square. At a binary vertex every contributing base in a convex representation equals that vertex, so the actual fibers are exactly the prescribed full-dimensional ones. The convex hull is full-dimensional because it has a full continuous fiber and full base span. The strict deletion witnesses have relatively open neighborhoods meeting their own triangles in positive area. The triangle has legs $15/4$ and area $225/32$. In its indexed normal direction the threshold $-1$ picks an apex subtriangle with scale $(5/2+1)/(5/2+5/4)=14/15$, hence area $49/8$. All other triangle fibers are missed. At $D$ four caps, the ones with threshold $-5$ or $-1$, contain the full square, while the other five miss it. Its area is $1/2500$, which gives the two masses and the total. Any threshold strictly between the largest individual mass and the total is a strict budget for this actual source cover.

Each binary base is exposed, so at any mark a sufficiently large finite base tilt of any chosen through-point own cap excludes every other compact fiber while keeping its own cut. Any containing cap always pays at least its own-fiber contribution. Thus the maximal mixed depth is the largest own ordinary maximal depth. For a triangle the normalized value is $4/9$ by ea91e021ff1f4416, and for the square it is $1/2$ by central symmetry and a direction through any mark choosing the smaller half. Their raw values are $25/8$ and $1/5000$, respectively. The displayed cap budgets therefore exceed the actual critical depth, which itself exceeds $M/9$.

For stability, each original one-from-each triple contains zero in the interior of its normal triangle, and every other subset of at most three normals misses zero in its convex hull (this includes the pairs). The properties persist by continuity and finiteness. Any minimal positive dependence in dimension two has at most three members, so exactly the same supports remain; their normalized weights vary continuously. The strict circuit signs at $A,B,C,D$, strict witnesses, and strict feasible point persist. Both the four original projected complementary inequalities and the nine original ambient complementary inequalities define nonempty bounded polyhedra. Hence each list of outward normals positively spans its ambient space: a nonzero common recession direction would contradict boundedness. The corresponding positive lower bound on the maximum normal evaluation over the unit sphere persists under small perturbations. With nearby bounded thresholds this yields uniform boundedness. If arbitrarily small perturbations admitted an integer point in the projected system, a bounded subsequence would converge to an integer point in the original, a contradiction. For every perturbation sufficiently small, the four continued projected inequalities therefore still miss the integer lattice, which gives the global mixed cover and excludes mixed points in the nine opposite inequalities as well. Strict feasibility and the deletion witnesses still make all nine opposite inequalities facets; the same witnesses on the fixed convex source still give positive exclusive area. All these properties are open near the displayed data, and the rational perturbations avoiding parallel copies are dense there.

statement:
Let $z=(z_1,z_2)$ and $x\in\mathbb R^2$, and put $u_0=(1,0)$, $u_1=(0,1)$, $u_2=(-1,-1)$. Use the nine caps $H_{gi}=\{u_i\cdot x\ge b_{gi}(z)\}$ for $g,i\in\{0,1,2\}$, where
$$
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
g&b_{g0}&b_{g1}&b_{g2}\\ \hline
0&-1+4z_1+4z_2&-1+4z_1+4z_2&-1+4z_1+4z_2\\
1&3-4z_1+14z_2&7-8z_1-4z_2&3-4z_1\\
2&3+14z_1-4z_2&3-4z_2&7-4z_1-8z_2
\end{array}
$$
The closed opposite polyhedron is bounded and full-dimensional, has all nine inequalities as facets, and is disjoint from $\mathbb Z^2\times\mathbb R^2$. Put $A=(0,0)$, $B=(1,0)$, $C=(0,1)$ and $D=(1,1)$. Any selection from these original caps by minimal positive continuous-normal circuits whose projected sides cover those four bases must include rows $0,1,2$ and the cross-triple $\{(0,0),(1,1),(2,2)\}$. These four groups already cover the full mixed lattice, and the fourth has no private cap, despite $9>2^2\cdot2$.

Take the convex hull of fibers $K=\operatorname{conv}\{(5/2,-5/4),(-5/4,5/2),(-5/4,-5/4)\}$ over $A,B,C$ and the square $[-1/100,1/100]^2$ over $D$. Its only integer fibers are the given ones. Each original cap has a positive-area portion of this source covered by no other cap. Its raw cap masses are $49/8$ or $49/8+1/2500$, its total mixed mass is $675/32+1/2500$, and its maximal mixed depth is $25/8$. The structural example persists under sufficiently small perturbations of all nine continuous normals and affine thresholds, including rational perturbations removing the parallel copies.
title: Nine essential caps can force a circuit without a private cap
